title: The Proxy Metric

scenario.situation: After a homepage redesign, average time-on-site rose 22% — but paid subscriptions fell 8% over the same four weeks.
scenario.stakeholderBelief: The product team reads the time-on-site lift as proof the redesign is working and wants to double down on the new layout.
scenario.question: Is rising time-on-site a genuine signal of value, or is something else going on?

decisions.prompt: The product team is celebrating the time-on-site lift. How do you frame your investigation?

options.label: Validate the time-on-site increase
options.detail: Confirm the 22% lift is real and statistically significant across user cohorts.
options.consequence: You confirm the lift is real — but you've only answered whether the proxy moved, not whether it means what the team thinks it means. The subscription drop remains unexplained.
options.divergenceCost: Anchored on validating the team's metric instead of questioning whether it reflects the real goal.

options.label: Diagnostic check: does the proxy still track the goal?
options.detail: Ask whether time-on-site and subscriptions are moving together or apart, then segment behavior to find where they diverge.
options.consequence: You immediately surface a divergence: the proxy and the real outcome are pointing in opposite directions. Segmenting session behavior reveals that the extra time is concentrated in navigation and search — not content consumption — suggesting friction, not value.

options.label: A/B re-test the redesign
options.detail: Run a fresh A/B test pitting the old layout against the new one.
options.consequence: You'll get clean data eventually, but the test takes weeks and the team is already shipping follow-on changes. You've also sidestepped understanding why subscriptions fell in the first place.
options.divergenceCost: Jumped to experimentation before diagnosing — slow and skips the root-cause question.

options.label: Attribute the subscription drop to seasonality
options.detail: Check whether subscription numbers always dip in this calendar period.
options.consequence: Historical data shows no consistent seasonal dip in this window, so you've spent time ruling out a factor that wasn't the culprit — and the team's confidence in the redesign is unshaken.
options.divergenceCost: Chased an alternative explanation without first testing whether the proxy itself had drifted.

decisions.prompt: You decide to segment session behavior to understand where the extra time is going. Which metric do you trust to confirm the real story?

artifact.title: Average time-on-site by activity type — post-redesign vs. pre-redesign (seconds)
artifact.caption: Raw average seconds per session in each activity type after the redesign. The biggest bars look like deep engagement — but are they?

options.label: Raw average time per activity type
options.detail: Compare how many seconds users spend in each activity category after the redesign.
options.consequence: Navigation and search look like engagement hotspots — but raw time doesn't tell you whether users chose to be there or got stuck. You might recommend leaning into navigation features that are actually friction points.
options.divergenceCost: Treated all time as equal engagement — couldn't distinguish value-seeking from floundering.

options.label: Subscription conversion rate by dominant session activity
options.detail: For each activity type, calculate the % of sessions dominated by that activity that ended in a subscription.
options.consequence: The picture flips: sessions dominated by content reading convert at 14%, but sessions dominated by navigation or search convert at under 2%. The redesign is routing users into high-time, low-value loops — the proxy has fully decoupled from the goal.

artifact.title: Subscription conversion rate by dominant session activity (%)
artifact.caption: Sessions where users spent most time navigating or searching barely convert. The redesign inflated time in the two lowest-converting activity types.

decisions.prompt: Sessions heavy in navigation and search convert at under 2%, while content-reading sessions convert at 14%. What do you tell the product team?

options.label: "The redesign broke discovery — revert it immediately."
options.detail: Make the causal call and recommend a rollback.
options.consequence: You sound decisive, but you've made a causal claim from observational data. Users who navigate a lot may differ from content readers in ways unrelated to the redesign. If the team reverts without a controlled test, they may fix nothing — and lose the goodwill of the design org.
options.divergenceCost: Overclaimed causation and recommended action without a causal test.

options.label: "Time-on-site is no longer tracking subscriptions — the extra time is correlating with low-conversion behavior. We should treat time-on-site as a flawed proxy going forward and run a holdout or A/B against the old layout before any further rollout."
options.detail: Report the proxy divergence, flag the causal gap, and recommend a controlled test.
options.consequence: You've reframed the team's success metric with evidence, named the proxy drift explicitly, and given them a concrete next step that doesn't require overclaiming. The team can act — and they understand what they're testing for.

insight: The redesign inflated time-on-site by making users hunt through menus and search filters — high-time, low-value behavior that looks like engagement but predicts churn. The lesson is not that time-on-site is always a bad metric, but that proxy metrics require periodic validation against the real goal they stand in for; when the two diverge, the proxy has stopped working. A sound analyst asks 'does this proxy still track the outcome?' before celebrating the proxy's rise.
